title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python
authors: Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani & Jonathan Taylor
why: Use this as the course’s statistical reference. Read the relevant chapter after the Atlas example, then work an exercise before opening its lab.
focus: Statistical learning, regression, classification, resampling, regularization, trees, SVMs and unsupervised learning. Skip the deep-learning chapter for this release.
task: Keep a model comparison sheet: assumptions, tuning controls, failure modes and evaluation procedure.
access: The authors provide a book PDF on their site. External material retains its own license.

title: Official ISLP Python labs
why: Connect the book’s ideas to real Python analysis. Read the lab, reproduce it locally, then change one modeling assumption and explain the effect.
focus: Select the lab matching the current topic; pay attention to data preparation and the evaluation setup, not only the estimator call.
task: Reproduce one figure or result with a changed seed and explain which conclusions remain stable.
access: External companion documentation. Package and dataset terms are provided by the authors.

title: Machine learning in Python with scikit-learn
authors: Inria Learning Lab and scikit-learn contributors
why: A strong companion for learning how to construct and criticize predictive pipelines. Recommended after basic Python.
focus: Predictive modeling, preprocessing, validation, parameter tuning, linear models, trees and ensembles.
task: For each notebook, identify exactly which objects learn from data and which subset each object may see.
access: Public course materials, notebooks, exercises and linked videos; the provider identifies the materials as CC BY.

title: Stanford CS229: Machine Learning
why: Use selected lectures and handouts when you can already follow the small example and want a more formal treatment.
focus: Supervised learning, generative algorithms, SVMs, learning theory, regularization, model selection and clustering. Follow only the classical-ML material here.
task: Rewrite one derivation using consistent dimensions, then verify a tiny numerical example independently.
access: Stanford hosts lectures and course handouts. Link to these materials; they are not bundled in ML Atlas.

title: Google Machine Learning Crash Course
why: An approachable second explanation when a first encounter with regression, classification or data preparation feels abstract.
focus: Use the regression, classification and working-with-data modules. Neural-network modules are outside this release.
task: Predict an interactive exercise’s result before changing a control; write down why the observed result differs.
access: Public learning modules on the provider’s website.

title: scikit-learn user guide
why: Use the estimator-specific guide to check assumptions and actual API behavior before turning an educational calculation into a project.
focus: Read the guide section, parameter definitions, warnings and linked examples for the model in use.
task: Record the fitted attributes and preprocessing requirements; do not infer behavior from an estimator’s name.
access: Public documentation. API details may differ from the pinned project version.

title: The Python Tutorial
why: A precise reference for the language features used in every lesson’s runnable calculation.
focus: Control flow, functions, data structures, errors, modules and environments.
task: Write a small transformation as a function and test it on empty, normal and malformed input.

title: NumPy absolute beginners guide
why: Build confidence in array shape and axis reasoning before treating vectorized code as a shortcut.
focus: Creation, indexing, axes, shape and broadcasting; follow with linear algebra reference pages.
task: Predict the shape of every intermediate array before executing it.

title: pandas getting-started tutorials
why: Learn to build trustworthy tables from raw records before fitting a model.
focus: Selection, derived columns, summaries, combining tables and time-series handling.
task: For a join, state the expected row count and check key uniqueness before and after it.

title: Random Forests (2001)
why: Read after building a single tree and a bagging example. It develops the role of randomized trees and their relationship to ensemble generalization.
focus: First read the introduction, algorithm description and experimental setup; return to the theoretical analysis after learning margins and probability.
task: Explain why reducing similarity between tree errors can help an average. Design a comparison that changes max_features while holding the split fixed.
access: Publisher landing page; full-text access depends on the provider. No PDF is redistributed here.

title: Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine (2001)
why: Connect the residual-fitting example to optimization over prediction functions, after you understand ordinary gradient descent.
focus: The least-squares case and stagewise additive procedure before other loss functions.
task: Derive the negative gradient of half squared error and show why it equals the residual. Explain the role of shrinkage.
access: Original journal article on the publisher’s site; no article text is bundled.

title: Support-Vector Networks (1995)
why: Read after the margin and slack-variable exercises to see the original formulation for nonseparable classification.
focus: Geometric margin, soft constraints and the role of transformed feature spaces.
task: Draw a point inside the margin but on the correct side of the boundary. Explain why it can incur loss without being misclassified.
access: Publisher landing page; full-text access depends on the provider. External rights remain with the authors/publisher.
